THE SESSION FLOW

One topic. A room of possibilities.

People create rich examples of physical behavior by handling objects, preparing food, and moving through everyday spaces. First-person video captures some of that experience. This proposed session uses EgoScale as a starting point to explore what a robot can learn from human observation—and what still requires action labels, alignment, and robot interaction.

A topical, speaker-led workshop will connect the data pipeline to robot transfer and evaluation. Afterward, exactly 15 minutes of pizza and spontaneous conversation will make room for questions and new connections. The final brainstorming segment is optional: stay to develop a research or startup idea, meet possible collaborators, and choose a next step together.

01 / SPEAKER-LED WORKSHOP

From a human view to a robot action.

A topic speaker will guide the technical walkthrough, with space to pause, compare approaches, and work through examples. The speaker is to be confirmed; the outline and exercises below are proposed.

  1. 01

    Read a first-person demonstration

    The speaker will unpack what egocentric data captures: objects, hand motion, scene context, and the order of actions. We will also identify what video alone may leave uncertain, including contact forces and the state of objects outside the camera view.

    Suggested exercise: break an everyday manipulation task into observations, actions, and missing information, without collecting anyone’s personal footage.

  2. 02

    Turn observations into aligned action data

    Use EgoScale to discuss action-labeled human data and the stages that connect human and robot experience. We will examine label quality, timing, embodiment differences, and why more video is not automatically a better robot training set.

    Suggested exercise: propose an annotation schema for one task and identify where a human-hand action needs a different representation for a robot.

  3. 03

    Test transfer, not just a familiar demo

    Connect the data choices to a target robot and a defensible evaluation. The workshop will distinguish performance on familiar tasks from transfer to new objects, settings, or embodiments, with human interventions recorded separately.

    Suggested exercise: sketch a held-out test split, a comparison baseline, and a failure log before deciding what a successful transfer result would mean.

02 / PIZZA & OPEN CONVERSATION

Put the slides aside.

15 MINUTES

After the workshop, we will take exactly 15 minutes for pizza, meeting new people, and free-form discussion. Join any conversation, compare notes with someone new, or bring up the question that did not fit into the workshop. There is no assigned group or required pitch.

Suggested conversation starters—not a record of questions asked:

  1. 01

    What useful information does egocentric video contain, and what action or physical-state information is missing?

  2. 02

    How should we compare more hours of data with better labels, greater diversity, or closer alignment to a target robot?

  3. 03

    Which human skills transfer across embodiments, and where do geometry, contact, and control differences become decisive?

03 / OPTIONAL BRAINSTORMING & TEAM FORMATION

Stay for the idea you want to pursue.

The final segment is for anyone who wants to turn the conversation into a research question or startup idea. Bring an idea, join someone else’s, or listen first. Participation and team formation are optional—you do not need a finished pitch or a team in advance.

  • Find a shared question. Say what interests you, who a solution might help, and what you would like to learn.
  • Meet possible teammates. Compare interests and skills, then decide whether you want to explore an idea together.
  • Choose a first test. Sketch a small experiment or prototype, the evidence it should produce, and what support the team might need.

Possible starting points

These are suggested project directions, not existing teams, announced projects, or reported outcomes.

  • Research direction

    An action-label quality study

    Plan a small comparison of annotation choices on appropriately licensed data, asking which labels are most useful for a clearly defined downstream task.

  • Research direction

    A transfer-evaluation scorecard

    Design a protocol that separates familiar-task success, new-object transfer, and human assistance, with a consistent way to record failures.

  • Startup direction

    A first-person data review tool

    Explore an interface for inspecting action labels, alignment errors, consent, and dataset permissions before footage enters a robot-learning pipeline.

AFTER THE SESSION / SUPPORT & FOLLOW-UP

An idea can keep going after the room clears.

Teams can discuss available PCPU support and agree on next steps. Resource support will depend on the project’s needs and what the organization can make available; this is not a promise of funding, equipment, or a fixed allocation.

PCPU will stay in touch with teams that choose to continue. Follow-up check-ins will give teams a place to share progress, surface blockers, and refine their next experiment or prototype. The check-in plan and any resource arrangements will be agreed with each team.

A PROMPT TO TAKE WITH YOU

What experiment would distinguish memorizing familiar tasks from generalizing to new objects, tasks, and robot bodies?
